profile.name: Neha Jha
profile.headline: Business Development Specialist with experience across tech, startups, legal, and product operations.
profile.intro: I'm a 3rd year student studying business and law with experience across big law firms, AI and tech startups, and more. I specialize in internal business development strategy & scaling organizations specifically in tech and engineering.

featuredWork.description: Built AI-enabled business development workflows, organized fragmented knowledge systems, and supported partner-facing research, reporting, and client opportunity tracking.
details: Mapped fragmented BD workflows across research, CRM, pitch materials, client intelligence, and event tracking to identify where professionals lose time switching between tools.
Designed an AI-assisted operating layer that helped turn scattered internal knowledge into a more usable decision interface for partner and BD use cases.
Supported alumni and client development work through CRM data cleanup, research, relationship tracking, and leadership-facing reports.
takeaways: The best AI use cases are not flashy. They remove friction from high-frequency workflows.
Institutional knowledge becomes more valuable when it is searchable, structured, and tied to real decisions.
Business development is not just outreach. It is research, timing, relationship intelligence, and operational discipline working together.

featuredWork.description: Created operating systems, onboarding workflows, alumni review cycles, and client compliance infrastructure for a 200+ member student product development studio.
details: Built centralized Notion systems across client teams to standardize project tracking, milestone visibility, documentation, and KPI monitoring.
Created client onboarding, contract, and compliance workflows to make external client work more professional, repeatable, and legally thoughtful.
Designed alumni product review cycles that connected experienced alumni with active teams for structured product feedback and sharper execution.
takeaways: Operations becomes strategic when it helps teams scale without losing quality.
A strong system should make the right behavior easier, not create more admin work.
Working with engineers taught me how important it is to translate business needs into clear, usable structures.

featuredWork.description: Built a regional partner pipeline from zero, supported GTM strategy, and helped shape outreach, onboarding, and customer discovery processes.
details: Built and managed partner sourcing workflows for local businesses across Boston and New York, moving outreach from one-off effort into a repeatable pipeline.
Helped refine pitch strategy, onboarding flows, and partner value propositions based on direct conversations with business owners.
Partnered with product and marketing workstreams to connect customer discovery insights back into website strategy and user journey decisions.
takeaways: Early-stage growth is mostly learning speed: talk to the market, adjust the pitch, and systemize what works.
A good GTM motion needs both creative storytelling and disciplined follow-through.
The cleanest product strategy usually comes from listening carefully to users before overbuilding.

featuredWork.description: Supported business research related to financial reporting while building a stronger foundation in academic research, source analysis, and structured analytical thinking.
details: Contributed to research support under Professor Lunawat at UCI in an academic business research context related to financial reporting.
Developed comfort with reading research questions carefully, organizing source material, and supporting analytical work with precision.
Used the experience to better understand the type of research environment I enjoy and how I want to connect future research to strategy, organizations, innovation, and business systems.
takeaways: Research made me more disciplined about how claims are formed and supported.
I learned that I enjoy analytical work most when it connects to strategy, organizational systems, and decision-making.
The experience gave me a stronger foundation for future research roles across business, innovation, and organizational design.

projects.title: AI Business Development Dashboard
projects.blurb: A centralized partner-facing decision layer designed to consolidate research, CRM insights, pitch materials, and opportunity signals into one workflow.
projects.summary: This project explores what a modern Marketing & Business Development hub could look like for a partner or BD professional who needs client intelligence quickly, cleanly, and in context.
strategy: The core idea was to reduce tool-switching. Instead of forcing users to jump between CRM, pitch repositories, legal research tools, market intelligence, event calendars, and AI tools, the dashboard brings the most common partner-facing questions into one interface.

I organized the product around four major needs: client intelligence, target clients and BD, events and networking, and resources/tools. Each section reflects a real workflow rather than a random feature list.
The design intentionally prioritizes quick scanning, relationship context, and mobile usability because BD decisions often happen right before meetings, events, or partner conversations.

projects.title: Client Operations Framework
projects.blurb: A repeatable onboarding, compliance, and milestone tracking system for product teams working with external clients.
projects.summary: A project focused on turning client work from informal student-team interactions into a more professional operating model with clearer expectations, documentation, and accountability.
strategy: The framework started with a simple problem: teams were doing client-facing work, but the standards around communication, scope, documentation, and checkpoints were not consistent enough across branches.

I treated client operations as both a business systems problem and a legal/compliance problem. That meant thinking about templates, handoffs, project charters, milestone reviews, contract language, and IP considerations together.
The goal was not to add bureaucracy. It was to create enough structure that teams could move faster with fewer misunderstandings.

projects.title: Alumni Product Review Program
projects.blurb: A structured review model connecting alumni expertise with active product teams to improve feedback loops and project quality.
projects.summary: A program designed to make alumni engagement more useful by connecting alumni directly to active product teams for structured reviews and targeted feedback.
strategy: Instead of treating alumni programming as purely social, I wanted alumni engagement to support the work happening inside client teams.
The review structure gave project leads a clear format: choose timing, submit project context and questions, present the product, and use alumni feedback to improve the next milestone.
The program created a more practical feedback loop between industry experience and student product execution.

posts.title: What I'm learning about AI, business development, and institutional knowledge
posts.excerpt: Thinking through how AI becomes useful when it is embedded directly into messy human workflows, not just placed on top of them.

sections.heading: The real problem is not lack of information.
sections.body: Most teams already have more information than they know what to do with. The issue is that the information lives across decks, inboxes, CRMs, documents, spreadsheets, and people's heads. AI becomes valuable when it helps connect those pieces into a workflow someone can actually use.

sections.heading: Useful AI has to sit inside the way people already work.
sections.body: A tool can be technically impressive and still fail if it asks people to change too much at once. The better approach is to understand the current workflow first, then use AI to remove friction from the moments that are already repetitive, research-heavy, or decision-heavy.

sections.heading: Institutional knowledge is a business asset.
sections.body: The more I work across business development and operations, the more I see institutional knowledge as infrastructure. When it is organized well, teams move faster, onboard faster, and make better decisions with less dependency on one person remembering everything.

posts.title: Why operations is not just admin work
posts.excerpt: The best operators do not just keep things moving. They create the systems that let good work repeat itself.

sections.heading: Operations is the difference between effort and repeatability.
sections.body: A lot of people think operations is just scheduling, documentation, or keeping things organized. Those things matter, but the deeper value is designing systems that make strong execution easier to repeat.

sections.heading: Good systems protect good work.
sections.body: When a team grows, informal communication starts breaking. The operator's job is to build enough structure that people know what matters, where things live, who owns what, and how decisions get made.

sections.heading: The best ops work feels invisible when it works.
sections.body: A strong operating system does not need to be loud. It shows up in fewer dropped balls, clearer handoffs, better meetings, cleaner onboarding, and a team that can scale without constantly reinventing the same process.

posts.title: Building a career across business, law, and tech
posts.excerpt: A personal map of how legal thinking, business development, and product strategy can fit together.

sections.heading: I like work that lives between disciplines.
sections.body: The most interesting problems rarely fit cleanly into one lane. Business, law, and technology all shape how companies grow, protect themselves, make decisions, and build products people actually use.

sections.heading: Legal thinking makes strategy sharper.
sections.body: Studying law has made me more careful with language, risk, incentives, and structure. That way of thinking is useful far beyond legal work because strong strategy depends on understanding constraints as much as possibilities.

sections.heading: The career thread is building better systems.
sections.body: Across startups, product teams, and professional services, I keep coming back to the same type of work: finding messy workflows, understanding what is broken, and building systems that help teams move with more clarity.
